faqs.q: Why are bats such a Durham issue in summer?
faqs.a: The housing stock and the trees. Older Durham homes offer the warm, gapped attics maternity colonies want, and summer is when colonies are largest and most noticeable. Bats are protected; exclusion happens only in the August 1 through April 30 window, by a licensed Wildlife Control Agent, with one-way devices and full sealing afterward. A colony found in June gets a plan and a calendar date, not a rushed job.

Durham.wildlife_intro:
Durham's canopy and age set its pattern: raccoons and squirrels working the historic neighborhoods' roofs, bats in the tobacco-era housing and big attics, and groundhogs in the open ground of the expanding edges.

The Eno and Ellerbe corridors thread opossums, skunks, and snakes through the city, Falls Lake's shore lots get the full lake-edge roster, and rats are a standing downtown and restaurant-corridor presence.

Wildlife pressure in Durham follows the green corridors — creeks, greenways, and unbroken canopy — straight to the rooflines. Spring litters fill attics and chimneys, summer colonies of bats settle the older housing under the state's protected season, and fall turns every unsealed vent into an application for winter tenancy. Our crew inspects roofline, attic, and foundation as one system, removes the animals present under the rules for each species, and seals the full entry set in the same visit's plan.

faqs.a: Shoreline concentration: raccoons working the banks nightly, opossums following, snakes in the rocks and brush at the water line, and rodents in the outbuildings above it. Our crew inspects the water-facing side of the property as carefully as the house, removes animals that have denned in structures, and seals the openings that face the lake.

Bahama.wildlife_intro:
Bahama's calls are reservoir-and-farm calls: raccoons around the lake woods and barns, groundhogs in the field edges, bats in the farmhouse attics, and opossums and skunks at every house the tree lines touch.

The Little River and Lake Michie shorelines concentrate snakes and rodents at the water's edge, and the quiet roads mean dead-animal and denning calls make up a bigger share here than in the city.

The Piedmont year runs in waves through Bahama. Cold months drive squirrels and rodents into attics, spring opens raccoon denning in chimneys and crawlspaces, and summer brings bat maternity colonies — protected statewide, with eviction by a licensed Wildlife Control Agent limited to August 1 through April 30. Autumn sends a second squirrel and rodent push for winter rooms. Our crew starts with a full roofline, attic, and crawlspace inspection, then removes the animals and seals every entry we find, because closing only the obvious hole rarely holds.

faqs.a: Because the animals use the whole property. A raccoon denning in the barn, rats at the feed shed, and squirrels in the house attic are one landscape with three tenants. Inspecting only the house leaves the sources standing. Our crew walks the full property, removes the animals in each structure under the rules for their species, and seals across the set.

Rougemont.wildlife_intro:
Rougemont work is deep-country work: raccoons in the barns and chimneys, groundhogs in the pasture ground, bats in the tall farmhouses, and snakes along the two rivers' bottoms.

The reservoir and river woods hold the full northern-Piedmont roster, and properties here are large enough that most calls involve outbuildings as well as the house.

In Rougemont the calendar is written by litters and weather. Raccoons den in spring, bats raise flightless young through summer when North Carolina law holds evictions to the August-through-April window, groundhogs and skunks work the ground from spring thaw to fall, and the first cold nights push rats and mice indoors. We inspect the whole envelope, read the sign to name the occupant, then remove and seal as one job — sequenced to the species, not to the week the noise started.
